messages.text: I had my baby 4 months ago. Me, my boyfriend and the baby. He makes $4,000/month. What can we apply for?

You can probably apply for all three. Here's what I found, and then I have two quick questions to firm up the food assistance part.

## What to apply for

**1. Health coverage (TennCare / CoverKids): likely for the baby**
- TennCare covers babies under 1 when household income before taxes is at or under about **$4,440 a month** for a family of 3. Your $4,000 is under that.
- CoverKids is a backup for children under 19. Its limit for 3 people is about **$5,692 a month**.
- It looks **possible** for you, since you're 4 months after giving birth. The page I opened didn't list a separate limit for new moms, so a caseworker will need to check this.
- It looks **unlikely** for your boyfriend. Tennessee's limit for parents is about **$2,277 a month**, and he's over it. He can still apply.
- Source: [TennCare/CoverKids income guidelines](https://www.tn.gov/coverkids/coverkids/redirect-income-guidelines.html)
- Apply at tn.gov/tenncare or call 1-855-259-0701. I got that number from a search result, not the page itself.

**2. WIC (food help and nutrition support for moms and babies): likely**
- Income can be up to 185% of poverty. Figures I found put that around **$4,100 to $4,200 a month** for 3 people. Your $4,000 is under both numbers.
- Both you and the baby are in the age and stage range for WIC.
- I couldn't open the official Tennessee or USDA WIC pages, so please confirm the exact limit when you apply. WIC will also do a quick health check.
- Call 1-800-DIAL-WIC, or ask 211 for your local WIC office. That number also came from a search result, not an official page I opened.

**3. Food assistance (SNAP): possibly**
- The usual federal limit for 3 people is about **$2,960 a month**, so $4,000 is over it.
- Tennessee may be using a higher limit of 200% of poverty, which is **$4,442 a month** for 3 people. At that limit, $4,000 is under. That change is reported by [TN Justice](https://www.tnjustice.org/post/bbce), an advocacy group. I couldn't find an official Tennessee page confirming it.
- Because the limit is unsettled, I can only say **possibly**. It's still worth applying.
- Even under the higher limit, your income after deductions (like rent and child care) has to be low enough. That's why I need the questions below.
- I couldn't open the official USDA 2026-27 tables, so I can't give a dollar estimate yet.

## Two questions
1. How much is your rent or mortgage each month? Do you pay for heat or air conditioning separately?
2. Is the $4,000 before taxes, and do you pay for child care so you or your boyfriend can work or study?

Only the agencies decide who gets help, and this is a first look, not a promise. You can still apply for any program, even if it looks unlikely. For free local help, call **211**.

Sources:
- [TennCare/CoverKids income guidelines](https://www.tn.gov/coverkids/coverkids/redirect-income-guidelines.html)
- [TN Justice: Tennessee SNAP BBCE change](https://www.tnjustice.org/post/bbce)
Rent is $1,100. Heat/AC is on a separate bill but I'm not sure exactly what it runs. Yes, $4,000 is before taxes. No child care.

With your rent, **food assistance (SNAP) looks unlikely**. You can still apply. WIC and TennCare/CoverKids are still your best bets.

## Food assistance (SNAP): unlikely

Even if Tennessee uses the higher limit I mentioned, your income after deductions also has to be under a second limit. Here is my rough math.

| Step | Monthly amount |
|---|---|
| Income before taxes | $4,000 |
| Minus 20% for work income | −$800 |
| Minus standard deduction (3 people, reported FY2027 figure) | −$217 |
| **Income after those deductions** | **about $2,983** |

- A rent and utility deduction only kicks in when your housing costs are more than half of that $2,983, which is about $1,490. Your rent is $1,100, and heat/AC probably brings you to around $1,400 to $1,500. That's right at the line, so it likely adds little or nothing.
- Tennessee's second limit is about **$2,277 a month** for 3 people. That is 100% of poverty, and [TN Justice](https://www.tnjustice.org/post/bbce) says Tennessee keeps this limit. The 100% figure itself is on the [CoverKids/TennCare page](https://www.tn.gov/coverkids/coverkids/redirect-income-guidelines.html). You'd be about $700 over it.
- The deduction and housing numbers come from search summaries of USDA's FY2027 update. I couldn't open USDA's official page or find Tennessee's heat/AC allowance. Treat this as an estimate.

Things that could change the result are child care costs, big medical bills for someone 60+ or disabled, child support you pay, or a drop in income. None of those apply to you right now. The caseworker does the final math, and you can still apply.

## Your best options

- **WIC:** likely for you and the baby. Your $4,000 is under the limit I found, which is about $4,100 to $4,200 a month for 3 people. Call 1-800-DIAL-WIC or 211 to find your local office.
- **TennCare/CoverKids for the baby:** likely. Babies under 1 can get TennCare up to about $4,440 a month for a family of 3. CoverKids goes up to about $5,692 a month.
- **TennCare for you:** possible, and a caseworker needs to look at it.
- **TennCare for your boyfriend:** unlikely, since the parent limit is about $2,277 a month.

Apply for TennCare and CoverKids at tn.gov/tenncare or at 1-855-259-0701. You can also call **211** for free help with any of these.

Only the agencies decide who gets help. If your income, rent, or household changes, you can check again or apply later.

Sources:
- [TennCare/CoverKids income guidelines](https://www.tn.gov/coverkids/coverkids/redirect-income-guidelines.html)
- [TN Justice: Tennessee SNAP BBCE change](https://www.tnjustice.org/post/bbce)

The search didn't turn up the official USDA FY 2027 income table, but secondary sources give the figures for a household of three.

- **Gross income limit (130% of poverty):** About $2,960 a month, or roughly $35,520 a year. This is derived from a federal FY 2027 poverty line of $2,277 a month for a three-person family, per the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (CBPP).
- **Net income limit (100% of poverty):** CBPP says net income must be at or below the poverty line, which for three people would be $2,277. No source gave the exact net figure for three, so treat this as derived.
- **Assets:** CBPP lists $3,000 or less for households without an elderly or disabled member, and $4,750 for households with one.
- **Cross-check on the FY 2027 figures:** Reports say the family-of-four gross limit is $3,575 and the single-person limit is $1,729 (up from $1,696). Both are consistent with the same poverty-line update.
- **Prior year (FY 2026), for comparison:** The USDA FY 2026 table lists $2,888 gross and $2,221 net for three people in the 48 states, D.C., Guam, and the Virgin Islands.

Some states use broad-based categorical eligibility, which can raise the gross limit above these federal figures. Households should check with their state SNAP agency. The official FY 2027 standards are on the USDA Food and Nutrition Service site (fns.usda.gov/snap/allotment/cola/fy27), which CBPP cites but I did not open.

For a household of 3 under the July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027 guidelines, the limit is about **$4,212 per month** or **$50,542 per year** (gross income). I couldn't find a Tennessee-issued table for this period yet.

It also says that household gross income must be equal to or less than WIC income guidelines (185% of Federal poverty).
- **Third-party calculators:** A poverty-calculator site lists $4,212 per month for three people, but it isn't an official source.

The sources agree on the broad structure, but the exact 2026 dollar figures conflict, and I didn't find the official TennCare income chart itself.

**Children (CoverKids):** CoverKids is Tennessee's CHIP program for children under 19 who are not eligible for TennCare. One guide puts its ceiling at 250% of the federal poverty level for 2026, which it says is $82,500 per year for a family of four. Another says CoverKids charges no monthly premium. A third source lists CoverKids at 250% FPL with small monthly premiums may apply, so the premium question is unresolved.

**Children (TennCare):** Figures differ by source. One lists up to 142% FPL (ages 1-5) or 133% FPL (ages 6-18), while another uses 138% FPL for ages 6 to 18.

**Parents and caretakers:** Most sources put the limit at 105% FPL. One says it is $2,391 a month for a family of three.

**Pregnant women and postpartum:** Official state data shows pregnancy coverage rose to 250% FPL on January 1, 2024. Coverage is for 12 months after the baby is born. The state's postpartum extension dates to April 1, 2022. Some 2026 guides still cite 200% FPL, which appears outdated.

**Adults without children:** Tennessee has not expanded Medicaid, so adults without children usually can't qualify at any income. Exceptions include pregnancy and disability.

**Caveats:** Several sources were updated in January or February 2026 and used 2025 poverty guidelines, with a note that these will increase in Spring 2026. A few commercial sites show different numbers, so verify against official sources. TennCare's member line is 1-855-259-0701, or visit www.tn.gov/tenncare.

Tennessee appears to have adopted BBCE in 2026, raising the gross income limit to 200% of the federal poverty level while keeping the net limit at 100%. The sources are mostly advocacy, news, and third-party sites, so the exact figures should be checked against TDHS.

- **Exemptions and net test:** A third-party calculator says households with a member age 60+ or receiving disability benefits are exempt from the gross income test. It also says net income must be at or below 100% FPL. Its figures are based on 2026 federal guidelines, and it advises to contact Tennessee DHS to confirm current thresholds.

I did not find an official TDHS or USDA page confirming the final 2026 numbers, so treat these as unverified until checked against TDHS directly.
